title: Cargo Bay Calibration
subtitle: Length, Mass, & Volume
tagline: The inventory robot's sensors are glitching. Recalibrate the scanner before the cargo bay overflows.

slides.headline: Warning: Sensor Malfunction
body: A heavy cargo ship just docked, but our inventory robot is completely glitching out. It's trying to measure the volume of a wrench and the length of our coolant water!
If it keeps logging these broken measurements, the cargo bay will overflow. The Math Cadet needs to take manual control of the Cargo Scanner and recalibrate the units.

slides.headline: What are we measuring?
slides.intro: Before you calibrate the scanner, you need to know which property to check.

cards.name: Length / Distance
cards.description: How long, wide, or far something is.

cards.name: Volume / Capacity
cards.description: How much space a liquid takes up.

prompt.question: Calibrate the scanner for this item.

correct.title: Lock Confirmed!
body: We use **Meters** to measure length. Millimeters are for tiny things (like a bug), and Kilometers are for long distances (like between cities).

config.instruction: Select what property to measure, then lock in the correct unit scale.
config.hint: A cargo door is pretty tall. You wouldn't want to measure it in tiny millimeters, but a kilometer is way too big.

correct.title: Mass Logged!
body: Heavy objects are measured in **Kilograms**. Grams are for light things like a paperclip, and Milligrams are for tiny amounts of medicine.

config.instruction: Lock in the correct property and unit for measuring something heavy.
config.hint: An engine is very heavy. You need the biggest unit of mass on this list.

correct.title: Volume Locked!
body: A large tank holds **Liters** of liquid. Milliliters are too small — you'd use those for a spoonful of medicine.

config.instruction: Lock in the correct property and unit for measuring a large liquid tank.
config.hint: A tank holds a lot of liquid. Think about a large soda bottle.

slides.headline: The Reasonableness Check
slides.intro: Even when the robot picks the right unit, the number might be totally wrong. Always ask yourself: **Does this make sense?**

rows.name: The "Too Big" Trap
rows.description: Logging a coffee cup as holding 5 Liters. (A 2-Liter soda bottle is huge — a coffee cup is much smaller!).

counter.label: CHECK
counter.text: Is the number too big for real life?

rows.name: The "Too Small" Trap
rows.description: Logging a spacesuit as weighing 5 grams. (A nickel weighs about 5 grams!).

counter.label: CHECK
counter.text: Is the number too small for real life?

prompt.scenario: The robot submitted one last cargo log. Perform a Reasonableness Check.
prompt.question: Which of these log entries is definitely BROKEN?

correct.title: Log Deleted!
body: Exactly! A single water bottle does not hold 400 liters (that's like a small swimming pool). The robot messed up.

opt-a.title: That one is fine!
body: A wrench is about 15 centimeters long (a bit shorter than a standard ruler). Try checking the other logs.

opt-b.title: That one is fine!
body: An adult astronaut weighing 80 kilograms makes perfect sense. Check the other logs.

wrongDefault.title: Math Trap
body: Think about how big these objects are in real life.

slides.headline: Mission Complete
slides.subtext: The Cargo Scanner is recalibrated and the station is fully supplied.
